title: latency-exposure-window-scratchpad
body:
Quick context:
This is a scratchpad tracking a set of small experiments to characterize the "exposure window" — the short period after a traffic surge during which p99 and tail latency remain elevated even when aggregate QPS returns to baseline. Goal is to understand mechanisms (batching hysteresis, kv-cache miss amplification, kernel warmup) and list mitigations we can test.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Model: redwood-7b-serve-v2 (fp16), small-quant variants tested in later runs
- HW: 1x A100-80GB (prod-like single-shard), CUDA 12, Triton-ish runtime + our continuous-batching layer
- Baseline steady-state: 80 qps sustained, seq_len=128 in/out tokens, 1.2ms token generation time average internal (for reference)
- Surge profile: 10s square pulse to 800 qps (10x peak), then immediate return to 80 qps
- Arrival distributions: instantaneous square pulse, Poisson ramp-up (tau 2s), and staircase (200 qps steps)
- Workloads: short-complete prompts (avg 60 tokens), a small set of deterministic prompts reused to test cache priming

Config knobs for this sweep:
- batch_timeout_ms: [4, 8, 16]
- max_batch_size: [32, 64, 128]
- kv_cache_enabled: [true, false]
- preemptive_eviction_threshold: [0.75, 0.9] (fraction of GPU mem)
- concurrency_limit_per_worker: [8, 16]

Key metric definitions captured:
- p50/p95/p99 response latency (end-to-end client observed)
- internal_dispatch_latency (time to schedule to GPU)
- avg_batch_size at token-start and token-continuation boundaries
- kv_cache_hit_rate (prefix hit fraction)
- cold_eviction_count (number of KV evictions during surge)
- downstream-queue-length (requests waiting to be batched)

Representative run: (square pulse 10s -> 800qps -> back to 80qps), config: batch_timeout_ms=8, max_batch_size=64, kv_cache_enabled=true, concurrency=16
- steady-state (pre-surge, 60s avg):
  qps: 80
  p50: 46 ms
  p95: 118 ms
  p99: 212 ms
  avg_batch_size: 12
  kv_cache_hit_rate: 0.87

- during surge (sustained 10s):
  qps: 800
  p50: 110 ms
  p95: 320 ms
  p99: 700 ms
  avg_batch_size: 56
  kv_cache_hit_rate: 0.61
  internal_dispatch_latency: +18 ms median

- immediate post-surge (first 30s after drop back to 80qps):
  qps: 80
  p50: 54 ms
  p95: 180 ms
  p99: 420 ms   <-- exposure window effect, significant tail carryover
  avg_batch_size: 34 (still elevated)
  kv_cache_hit_rate: 0.66 (rebuilding)
  cold_eviction_count: 9

Observation notes:
- The tail persists for ~25-40s after traffic normalizes in most square-pulse runs. The elevated avg_batch_size post-surge suggests batching hysteresis: once large batches form, the system continues to coalesce for longer than necessary because queue smoothing/backpressure isn't aggressive enough.
- KV cache hit rate drops sharply during surge and takes time to converge back. A small set of popular prefixes are evicted during the surge and then cause replays that produce heavy compute and further queuing.
- Preemptive eviction helps in some runs but can increase p50 during surge if done too aggressively. There's a balance.
- With batch_timeout_ms=4 the exposure window reduced ~30% but we saw slightly higher p95 under sustained surge due to more small batches (i.e., tradeoff).

Mini table: exposure-window length (sec) by batch_timeout_ms
- batch_timeout_ms=4 -> exposure_window median 18s
- batch_timeout_ms=8 -> exposure_window median 28s
- batch_timeout_ms=16 -> exposure_window median 44s

Ascii spark (post-surge p99 trend, one representative run):
p99: |700|620|580|520|480|450|430|420|410|405|402|400|395|390|387|385|383|381|380|379|378|377|376|375|
(time ticks: every 2s)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Batching hysteresis is primary: large batches created during surge do not drain immediately; subsequent baseline traffic gets coalesced into suboptimal waiting windows leading to higher tail.
2) KV cache eviction amplification: eviction during surge causes a cascade of cache-miss-powered cold token-generation which contributes disproportionately to tail.
3) Scheduling/worker-thaw latency: kernel selection and CUDA context warmup for certain quantized kernels adds ~10-20ms when rebalancing shards after surge.

Immediate mitigations to prototype:
- Adaptive batch_timeout: reduce timeout for X seconds after a detected drop in qps (aggressively favor small batches during the exposure window).
- Soft-cache-hold: protect top-K prefixes from eviction for Y seconds after a surge (small memory reservation).
- Eviction backoff: when eviction rate spikes, temporarily throttle new evictions and preferentially allocate burst cache to long-lived prefixes.

Experiments to run (next week):
1) Adaptive batch_timeout prototype: implement stateless switch that halves batch_timeout for 30s after a downward qps-crossing event. Measure exposure window and p95/p99.
2) Sticky-prefix reservation: reserve 5% GPU mem for top-100 prefixes; test with same surge profile. Observe kv_cache_hit_rate and p99 delta.
3) Mixed run with small-quant model variant to see if quant kernel warmup changes exposure window length.

Instrumentation notes / chase list:
- Add a per-batch token-size histogram to help understand whether post-surge batches are token-heavy (longer generation) or simply larger width.
- Trace correlation id from eviction events -> first request that misses after eviction to quantify miss amplification.
- Add sampling of CUDA kernel init times to identify scheduling warmup spikes.

Open questions:
- How common are square-pulse style microbursts in prod? We need to check traffic traces (TODO: ask data infra for 7-day ingress traces, filter by tenant).
- Is the exposure window effect visible for embeddings-only pipelines? Intuition: less internal token streaming, might be shorter.

Quick conclusions so far:
- Exposure window is real, reproducible across different arrival shapes, and is dominated by batching hysteresis + kv-cache rewarm.
- Short-term wins likely come from adaptive batching + small protections for hot prefixes.
- There are tuning tradeoffs: lower batch_timeout reduces tail post-surge but increases cost during sustained surges. Need a policy that responds to rate-of-change, not just absolute rate.

TODOs (owner tags):

- [Rory] prototype prefix-reservation scheduler, mock in sim first.

Notes-to-self: keep this file messy. Save raw JSON traces to /tmp/exposure-run-YYYYMMDD-*.gz and link into GH PR when I open it.

End of scratchpad.
